# Results — Study 1014 (The Perfect Macro Forecaster) on the real quarterly tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). As-of **2009-09-30** (the last
full quarter of the macro tape). Panel 1959-06-30 → 2009-09-30, 202 quarters;
evaluation window 1964-12-31 → 2009-03-31, **178 quarters**, identical for every rule.*

**Data provenance.**

| Tape | Source | Pin | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Macro — real GDP, unemployment, CPI inflation, T-bill rate | `statsmodels` 0.15.0 `datasets.macrodata` — **final vintage (revised)**, quarterly 1959Q1–2009Q3 | `macrodata.csv` SHA-256 `d93c0d3a7a77ef83…` (matched: True) | `1e7b301ae856` |
| Equity — US market **total return** and one-month T-bill | `arch` 8.0.0 `frenchdata` (Fama-French `Mkt-RF + RF`, CRSP value-weighted), monthly compounded to quarters | `frenchdata.csv.gz` SHA-256 `f23436727b01d879…` | `b8c123a09e7e` |

Panel fingerprint `6008ef31746a` (`quantlab.bundled.fingerprint` of `mkt, rf, g, du, infl, dtb`).

**The rule.** Before quarter *t*, the oracle reveals the final-vintage value of one variable for
quarter *t + h*. The investor holds the market over quarter *t* if that value is on the "good"
side (higher GDP growth; lower unemployment change, inflation, T-bill change) of the variable's
own **expanding, past-only median** (20-quarter warm-up), and T-bills otherwise. The combined
oracle is a majority vote of GDP, unemployment and inflation. One execution lag (position set at
the close of *t − 1*), costs **10 bps one-way × NAV traded**, all Sharpes are
**net**, annualised, excess of the bill rate, and compared against buy-and-hold excess returns on
the same quarters. Two nulls: a circular block bootstrap of the paired Sharpe difference (blocks
of 4 quarters, 2000 draws, centred, one-sided) and a rotation placebo (the oracle's own
positions shifted against the returns by every offset ≥ 4 quarters). The Newey-West *t* (4 lags)
of the active return is reported alongside.

| real GDP growth | -0.05 (-0.7) | -0.13 (-2.1) | -0.12 (-1.8) | -0.03 (-0.4) | +0.07 (+0.8) | +0.27 (+3.6) | +0.34 (+4.4) | +0.20 (+2.5) | +0.13 (+2.1) |
| unemployment change | +0.06 (+0.9) | +0.10 (+1.7) | +0.13 (+1.6) | +0.14 (+1.9) | +0.06 (+0.6) | -0.22 (-2.8) | -0.36 (-5.4) | -0.40 (-6.9) | -0.26 (-5.3) |
| CPI inflation | -0.05 (-0.7) | -0.15 (-1.6) | -0.04 (-0.4) | -0.08 (-1.0) | -0.13 (-1.2) | -0.08 (-0.9) | -0.01 (-0.2) | +0.01 (+0.1) | -0.02 (-0.4) |
| T-bill change | -0.06 (-0.8) | -0.05 (-0.7) | -0.05 (-0.9) | -0.13 (-2.3) | -0.10 (-1.5) | +0.18 (+3.4) | +0.17 (+2.7) | +0.01 (+0.2) | +0.05 (+1.0) |

Stocks lead the economy. The same-quarter correlation with GDP growth is
+0.07; it peaks one to two quarters **later**
(+0.27, +0.34), and unemployment is a mirror image a
quarter further out still. The backward-looking columns (k < 0) are where a real investor
lives, and they are much weaker; the one exception worth naming is the T-bill rate, a market
price that is never revised.

## 3. Same quarter vs one quarter beyond — the market prices the future

| Oracle | Sharpe, h=0 | Sharpe, h=+1 | Difference | 95% CI | p (h=+1 ≤ h=0) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GDP growth | 0.21 | 0.58 | **+0.37** | [+0.12, +0.64] | 0.004 |
| **combined (GDP+jobs+CPI)** | 0.29 | 0.47 | **+0.18** | [-0.00, +0.38] | 0.043 |

A perfect forecast of the quarter you are about to hold is worth little, because during that
quarter the market is busy pricing the *next* one. Move the oracle one quarter further out and
it starts to beat buy-and-hold. The macro-forecasting industry forecasts the quarter ahead; on
this tape that is precisely the horizon the market has already discounted.

## 4. The release-lag version — what you could actually have known

The combined oracle at h = −1 (last quarter's prints, available — generously — at the start of
the quarter) earns **0.48** vs 0.25 (ΔSharpe
+0.23, bootstrap p = 0.084, rotation p = 0.006,
NW *t* of the active return +0.06). The Sharpe gain comes from sitting out
volatile quarters, not from extra return: the active return itself is indistinguishable from
zero. With one more quarter of lag (h = −2) it earns **0.13** (ΔSharpe
-0.12) — the edge does not survive a one-quarter change in a parameter nobody
could choose with hindsight.

Costs barely matter at about one switch a year:

| 10 | 0.48 | +0.23 | 0.089 |
| 25 | 0.46 | +0.21 | 0.106 |
| 50 | 0.44 | +0.18 | 0.134 |

## 5. The ceiling — perfect foresight of the market itself

The market oracle, then the same oracle corrupted at random (200 patterns per row):

| Market-oracle hit rate | Sharpe | ΔSharpe vs B&H |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 100% | 1.53 | +1.27 |
| 90% | 1.17 | +0.92 |
| 80% | 0.87 | +0.62 |
| 70% | 0.62 | +0.36 |
| 60% | 0.38 | +0.13 |

The headline macro oracle calls the market's direction right in **51%** of
quarters and captures **+3%** of the gap between buy-and-hold and the ceiling;
the one-quarter-beyond oracle 56% and +17%. Perfect knowledge of the coming quarter's economy is worth **less** to an equity timer than a market oracle that is wrong four quarters in ten (ΔSharpe +0.04 vs +0.13).

## 6. Synthetic control — does the machinery work?

Deterministic worlds (400 quarters, ten seeds each) in which the excess return loads on the
standardised GDP growth of the **next** quarter (`signal_strength = 1`), and their matched nulls
(`0`): same macro paths, returns independent of them. The GDP oracle at h = +1 is run through
the full harness (net of costs, both nulls).

| Strength | Seeds | Mean Sharpe, GDP h=+1 | Mean B&H | Mean ΔSharpe | Median bootstrap p | Clears both nulls | Lead-lag \|t\| > 2 at k=+1 |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1.0 | 10 | 0.71 | 0.30 | +0.41 | 0.000 | **100%** | 100% |
| 0.0 | 10 | 0.23 | 0.33 | -0.10 | 0.758 | **0%** | 30% |

The harness banks the planted lead in every planted world and never certifies a null one. The
lead-lag Newey-West *t* is correctly sized: across 300 null seeds it rejects
at |t| > 2 in **6.0%** of them (nominal 5%; the ten-seed column above
is a small sample). This is a machinery proof, not market evidence.

## Caveats

- **Final vintage is the whole story for the realistic leg.** `macrodata` holds GDP as revised
  years later, not the advance estimate published about four weeks after each quarter. Real-time
  GDP growth differs from the final number by more than a percentage point (annualised) often
  enough to flip an above/below-median call (Croushore & Stark 2001 built the real-time dataset
  for exactly this reason). The T-bill rate is a market price and is never revised; CPI is barely
  revised; unemployment moves only with seasonal factors. The h = −1 and h = −2 rows are
  therefore an **upper bound** on what a real investor could have done, and the Tradability stamp
  is capped at Fragile by construction.
- **The release lag is generous.** h = −1 assumes last quarter's GDP is known at the start of the
  quarter; the advance estimate actually arrives about a month in. h = −2 is the strict version.
- **One rule family.** Above/below a past-only median, all-in or all-out. A regression-weighted
  or graded rule could extract more from the same foresight; the ceiling bounds what any rule
  could get.
- **Many cells.** 25 oracle × horizon cells were run. The verdict keys off three
  cells fixed in advance (combined oracle at h = 0, +1, −1), not the best cell.
- **Quarterly sampling.** Timing within the quarter (e.g. acting on monthly payrolls) is a
  different question, covered by neighbouring studies on this desk.
- **1964–2009, US only.** Fifty years, about eight recessions — not many independent episodes for
  a rule that trades about once a year.

## Verdict

Produced by `strategy.verdict`, fixed before the run and unit-tested in
[`tests/test_strategy.py`](../tests/test_strategy.py).

**Signal: None.** A flawless forecast of the **coming quarter's** GDP growth, unemployment change and inflation (combined oracle, h = 0) timed the market to Sharpe **0.29** vs 0.25 buy-and-hold, ΔSharpe +0.04, bootstrap p = 0.40, rotation p = 0.12 — indistinguishable from simply holding the market. The value lives further out: knowing the quarter *after* the holding quarter (h = +1) gives Sharpe **0.47** vs 0.25 buy-and-hold, ΔSharpe +0.22, bootstrap p = 0.09, rotation p = 0.01, and GDP alone at h = +1 gives Sharpe **0.58** vs 0.25 buy-and-hold, ΔSharpe +0.33, bootstrap p = 0.02, rotation p = 0.01. The market spends each quarter pricing the next one, so a perfect forecast of the quarter you are in arrives already priced. Stamped on the pre-registered headline (h = 0); the one-quarter-beyond oracle also failed to clear both nulls at 5%, so the split by horizon is suggestive, not certified.

**Tradability: Fragile.** What a real investor actually has is last quarter's print after the release lag (h = −1) — and even that on revised data nobody saw at the time. Net of 10 bps a switch it gave Sharpe **0.48** vs 0.25 buy-and-hold, ΔSharpe +0.23, bootstrap p = 0.08, rotation p = 0.01; one more quarter of lag (h = −2, data comfortably published before the quarter starts) gives Sharpe **0.13** vs 0.25 buy-and-hold, ΔSharpe -0.12, bootstrap p = 0.80, rotation p = 0.56. The perfect *market* oracle reaches **1.53**; the headline macro oracle captures **3%** of the gap between buy-and-hold and that ceiling, the one-quarter-beyond oracle 17%. A thin, lag-sensitive edge on final-vintage data is the definition of Fragile, and the vintage problem caps this stamp there whatever the numbers say.

**Stocks lead the economy? Confirmed.** The excess return's correlation with real GDP growth is +0.07 in the same quarter (t = +0.8) but +0.27 one quarter later (t = +3.6) and +0.34 two quarters later (t = +4.4).

> **In one sentence:** Even a flawless forecast of the coming quarter's GDP, jobs and inflation would have timed US stocks to a Sharpe of 0.29 against 0.25 for buying and holding, because the market had already moved on to pricing the quarter after — only an oracle that sees that far (0.47) starts to earn its fee; the lagged rule a real investor could run looks better on paper (0.48) but loses to buy-and-hold with one more quarter of lag (0.13).
